name: Environmental Defense Fund: health and nature (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: by share of the result at the defaults. EPA's soot and lead-pipe rules in the US (99%); fisheries reforms, split by judgment between Mexico and Indonesia, EDF's largest fisheries countries (0.8%); farm tonnes, spread by world population (0.2%).
summary: The Environmental Defense Fund's health and nature work (air pollution, lead and toxic chemicals; oceans, fisheries, farms, water and resilience: $78.2M in its year to September 2025, {{row:program_spend}} with its share of core capacities) is modelled from the policies it helped win in October 2021 to September 2025: EPA's 2024 soot standard (about {{row:pm_deaths_per_year}} deaths a year avoided, between EPA's two estimates; upheld in court in 2026) and lead-pipe rule (up to 1,500 deaths and 200,000 IQ points a year), fisheries reforms and farm emissions. At the defaults it gives about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000 after the two rules' compliance costs (EPA's own figures), over half from the soot standard and most of the rest from the lead-pipe rule; it is low because EDF is one of many groups behind each rule (credited with 10% and 20%), advocacy is credited with only part of a rule, the deaths it averts are mostly of older adults, the benefits come years later and the soot standard's roll-out has stalled. The biggest uncertainties are the shared years a won reform counts, the missing-data discount and EDF's shares of the two rules; every branch is discounted for missing data, and the fisheries and farm branches, small here, rest on judged reach.

Hectares protected (none counted here)
rows.explainer: EDF doesn't buy or protect land; its nature work is rules and practices (fisheries, farms, water), modelled in the branches below.

rows.label: EPA soot standard (2024): deaths a year avoided once in effect
rows.explainer: The shared figure for this rule (facts: climate): {{row:pm_deaths_per_year}} a year (1,900 to 5,700), between the two estimates of EPA's regulatory impact analysis for 2032, 4,500 for all adults and 2,100 for the over-64s.

rows.label: EPA lead-pipe rule (2024): heart-disease deaths a year avoided once lead pipes are replaced
rows.explainer: EPA's Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (October 2024) require nearly all lead service lines replaced within ten years; EPA puts the yearly benefit at up to 1,500 fewer premature deaths from heart disease once the rule is fully in place. Its heart-disease benefits range ($7.70 to $17.04 billion a year, Table 2) runs to 45% of the top. Our judgment, 1,100 a year (680 to 1,500).

source.title: US EPA (2024), Final Lead and Copper Rule Improvements: technical fact sheet, summary of benefits and costs (EPA 816-F-24-008)
source.page: Table 1, p. 1
source.quote: Annually, the rule will protect up to 900,000 infants from low birthweight, prevent up to 2,600 children from experiencing Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), reduce up to 1,500 cases of premature death from heart disease, and prevent up to 200,000 IQ points lost in children.

rows.label: EPA lead-pipe rule: IQ points a year not lost by children
rows.explainer: EPA: up to 200,000 IQ points a year not lost by children once the rule is fully in place; its IQ benefits run from $5.62 to $7.68 billion a year, so the low end is 73% of the top. Our judgment, 175,000 (146,000 to 200,000). ADHD and low birthweight, about 2% of EPA's value, are left in the other wins' share.

source.title: US EPA (2024), Final Lead and Copper Rule Improvements: technical fact sheet, summary of benefits and costs (EPA 816-F-24-008)
source.page: Tables 1 and 2, pp. 1-2
source.quote: Annually, the rule will protect up to 900,000 infants from low birthweight, prevent up to 2,600 children from experiencing Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), reduce up to 1,500 cases of premature death from heart disease, and prevent up to 200,000 IQ points lost in children.

rows.label: Fisheries: fishers in fisheries that moved to science-based limits and secure access with EDF's help in the period
rows.explainer: EDF's oceans programme works with governments and fishing communities on catch limits and secure fishing rights (managed access, catch shares) in Mexico, Belize, Indonesia, the Philippines, Peru, Chile, Cuba, Japan, the US and elsewhere (note 1, p. 13: EDF Indonesia works 'closely with the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries'). It publishes no count of fishers newly covered in 2022-2025. Our judgment, 100,000 (20,000 to 500,000): a few national reforms and dozens of local ones, each covering thousands to tens of thousands of small-scale fishers.

rows.label: People whose income changes (fishers)
Farm emissions: tonnes of CO₂e a year cut by practices and rules EDF's agriculture work brought in
rows.explainer: EDF works on fertiliser (nitrous oxide) in the US Midwest, rice and livestock methane in India and China, and on US farm programmes; the largest, USDA's $3.1 billion Partnerships for Climate-Smart Commodities (2022), was cancelled in 2025. EDF publishes no tonnes for the period. Our judgment, 1 million tonnes a year (0.1 to 5 million), a small fraction of the US farm sector's 600 million.

rows.label: People whose health is counted directly in DALYs (none: deaths and IQ are valued in units of value)
People whose life satisfaction gains from nature (not counted)
rows.explainer: Not counted: no study links EDF's fisheries or water work to measured life satisfaction.

rows.label: Wild fish-years changed (not counted)
rows.explainer: Fisheries limits leave more fish in the sea; whether a wild fish's life is better or worse than none is unknown, so their welfare is left out (0).

rows.label: Share of each won rule due to advocacy at all (all groups together)
rows.explainer: The shared figure for a won policy (facts: climate.advocacy_share_of_policy_win, 30%, 10% to 60%); its reference class, Burstein & Linton's review and Baumgartner et al.'s 98 lobbied issues, is policy in general, not only climate, so it serves the health, fisheries and farm rules too. EDF's part of the advocates' work is each branch's attribution row.

rows.explainer: The shared wait for rules and programmes (3 years, 1 to 6).

Tonnes of CO₂e per hectare a year (no land counted)
Value of a heart or lung death at 70 or older (units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's five-year weights for 70-74 and 75-79 (their mean) and for 80 and over, mixed by the share of US cardiovascular deaths at 70 or older that are at 80 or older (families/high-income-care.md).

rows.label: Value of an adult heart or lung death averted in the US (units of value)
rows.explainer: The ages of US cardiovascular deaths (facts: death_ages, GBD 2023: 74% at 70 or older) valued by GiveWell's weights by age, × the value-of-a-life slider. EPA's soot deaths are mostly heart and lung deaths of older adults, and the lead-pipe rule's are heart-disease deaths, so both branches use it.

rows.label: EPA soot standard: value of a death averted
rows.explainer: The US value of a heart or lung death (row above).

rows.label: EPA soot standard: years lived with illness averted per death averted
rows.explainer: Illness comes with the deaths (heart attacks, strokes, lung disease): the shared share of a rich country's cardiovascular DALYs that is illness (cvd_yld_share_gbr, 14%) over its deaths per DALY (cvd_deaths_per_daly_gbr), so both describe one population; the UK stands in for the US, the nearest the facts hold. About {{row:pm_illness_dalys_per_death}} healthy years of illness per death, counted in healthy years (row pm_illness_dalys).

rows.label: EPA soot standard: years from the win (2024) until the deaths are avoided
rows.explainer: The shared figure for this rule (facts: climate): 9 years from 2024 (7 to 11); EPA assumed attainment in late 2032 after designations in late 2025, and designations are now due by February 2027.

rows.label: EPA soot standard: discounted years of impact
EPA soot standard: expected units of value from deaths, before adjustments
EPA soot standard: expected illness averted before adjustments (DALYs)
EPA lead-pipe rule: value of an adult heart-disease death averted
rows.explainer: The US value of a heart death (rows above).

rows.label: EPA lead-pipe rule: years lived with illness averted per heart-disease death averted
rows.explainer: The same shared cardiovascular figures as the soot standard's (cvd_yld_share_gbr over cvd_deaths_per_daly_gbr, the UK standing for the US): heart attacks and strokes survived come with the deaths averted.

rows.label: Increase in earnings per IQ point
rows.explainer: The shared figure (GiveWell, {{row:iq_wage_gain}} per IQ point), read as a gain in ln(consumption).

rows.label: Household sharing multiplier on an earnings gain
rows.explainer: The shared multiplier for later-life income gains shared within the household (facts: givewell_shared).

rows.label: Years an IQ gain raises earnings, discounted
rows.explainer: The shared working life of 40 years (facts: givewell_shared.long_term_benefit_years), discounted.

rows.label: EPA lead-pipe rule: years from a child's lower exposure to working age
rows.explainer: The IQ points are children's, mostly under seven; they earn from about 20. Our judgment, 15 years (10 to 20), on top of the wait for the pipes.

rows.label: EPA lead-pipe rule: units of value a year from IQ points not lost
rows.explainer: Each year's IQ points × the earnings gain per point over a working life, discounted to the child's exposure, at the shared value of a doubled income.

rows.label: EPA lead-pipe rule: years from the win (2024) until the benefits come
rows.explainer: Utilities must start replacing in November 2027 and finish within ten years; the middle of the replacements is about 2032, eight years after the rule. Our judgment, 8 years (5 to 11).

source.title: US EPA (2024), National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI), final rule, 89 FR 86418 (30 October 2024)
source.note: Compliance from 1 November 2027; most systems must replace lead and galvanized service lines within 10 years of that date.

rows.label: EPA lead-pipe rule: discounted years of impact
EPA lead-pipe rule: expected units of value before adjustments
EPA lead-pipe rule: expected illness averted before adjustments (DALYs)
Fisheries: gain in ln(consumption) a year for a fisher under the new management
rows.explainer: No income evaluation of these reforms was found. Catch limits with secure access let stocks recover (Costello, Gaines & Lynham 2008, Science 321: catch-share fisheries half as likely to collapse), raising catch value once they do; in the first years fishers may catch less, and fishing is only part of most small-scale fishers' income. Our judgment, +0.5% a year (−0.5% to +3%).

rows.label: Fisheries: years from the reform until the income gain
rows.explainer: Stocks take a few years to recover. Our judgment, 3 years (1 to 6).

rows.label: Fisheries: discounted years of impact
Fisheries: expected units of value before adjustments
Farm emissions: expected tonnes before adjustments

Life-satisfaction gain per person-year (not counted)
Pain days per wild fish-year changed (not counted)
Deaths in a catastrophe the work lowers (none counted)
rows.explainer: EDF's health and nature work isn't credited with lowering a global catastrophe's chance.

rows.label: Cut in a catastrophe's yearly chance (none counted)
Value of a death in a catastrophe (none counted; the shared value of an older adult's death)
rows.explainer: Unused here (no catastrophe counted); kept so the template's rows stay whole.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment: how far the regulators' estimates and the judged reach should be trusted
rows.explainer: EPA's IQ points and lead deaths rest on large cohort studies (strong evidence that lead harms) and on its own exposure modelling, which can run high or low; the fisheries and farm reach are judgments. Our judgment, 0.8 (0.5 to 1.1), as for the climate rules' tonnes; the soot standard reads the rule's shared evidence row, and delivery and repeal are in each branch's implementation row.

rows.label: EPA soot standard: evidence adjustment on EPA's deaths
rows.explainer: The shared figure for this rule (facts: climate): 1 (0.7 to 1.2); the doubt about EPA's two estimates is already in the shared deaths figure.

rows.label: EPA soot standard: share of the deaths that wouldn't have been avoided anyway
rows.explainer: The shared figure for this rule (facts: climate): {{row:pm_counterfactual_adj}} (70% to 100%); EPA's baseline already holds the rules then in force.

rows.label: EPA soot standard: EDF's share of the advocacy resources behind the win
rows.explainer: EDF and the Moms Clean Air Force pressed for a strong standard and EDF intervened to defend it in the D.C. Circuit (upheld 26 June 2026), beside the American Lung Association, Earthjustice, NRDC, Sierra Club, the Clean Air Task Force and community groups; EPA's science advisers backed a tighter limit, and industry lobbied against it. Our judgment, 10% (4% to 25%).

source.title: EDF (2025), Trump's EPA abandons defense of national soot standard that saves lives
source.note: The D.C. Circuit upheld the standard and denied EPA's motion to vacate it on 26 June 2026 (Bloomberg Law, 'Court rejects Trump EPA bid to roll back soot pollution limit').

rows.label: This charity's share of the good done with money, work or budgets it brings in
rows.explainer: The site's one setting for resources another party commits only because of the organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.24): governments' budgets and enforcement, companies' compliance, the use others make of research. The charity is credited this share of the good done with them, net of their cost; the rest stays with those who paid or did the work. Fixed.

rows.label: EPA soot standard: share of credit used
EPA soot standard: share of the win's deaths avoided
rows.explainer: The shared figure for this rule (facts: climate): 50% (20% to 80%); upheld in June 2026, but EPA means to reconsider it, states have gone to the Supreme Court and designations are late.

rows.label: EPA lead-pipe rule: share of the benefits that wouldn't have come anyway
rows.explainer: Some cities and states were already replacing lead lines (Illinois, Michigan, New Jersey require it; the 2021 infrastructure law gave $15 billion), and EPA's baseline holds the 2021 rule. Our judgment, 75% (50% to 95%).

rows.label: EPA lead-pipe rule: EDF's share of the advocacy resources behind the win
rows.explainer: EDF's health team pressed for full replacement of lead service lines for a decade (analyses of the lines' numbers and costs, petitions, comments on the 2021 and 2024 rules) and sits on the steering committee of the Lead Service Line Replacement Collaborative, a forum of public health, water utility, environmental and housing groups (a forum for communities replacing lead lines). Others pressing for the rule: NRDC (Flint and Newark litigation), Earthjustice, the BlueGreen Alliance, community groups and parts of the water industry. Reference class: EDF was one of the three to five national groups that led on the file, against many smaller ones. Our judgment, 20% (8% to 35%).

source.title: Lead Service Line Replacement Collaborative, About Us (archived 14 January 2026)
source.note: The members list marks the Environmental Defense Fund as a steering-committee member (with the American Water Works Association, the Children's Environmental Health Network, Clean Water Action and others); the Collaborative helps communities replace lead lines. EDF's release of 8 October 2024 (https://www.edf.org/media/edf-applauds-historic-us-epa-rule-eliminate-lead-pipes) welcomes the rule.

rows.label: EPA lead-pipe rule: share of credit used
EPA lead-pipe rule: share of the win's benefits delivered
rows.explainer: The rule stands and EPA's implementation materials work to its ten-year deadline, but federal funding for lead lines ends in 2026, small systems get leeway and lines the utility can't reach are excused. Our judgment, 60% (35% to 85%).

source.title: US EPA, Lead and Copper Rule implementation tools
source.note: EPA's implementation materials for the 2024 rule (line access, inventories, replacement plans); the ten-year deadline itself is in the final rule (89 FR 86418).

rows.label: Side effect: lead released while pipes are dug up, as a share of the lead-pipe branch
rows.explainer: Replacing a lead line briefly raises lead at the tap, worst for partial replacements, which the rule bans; it requires filters and flushing after replacement. Our judgment, −1% of the branch (−3% to 0).

rows.label: Fisheries: share of the gain that wouldn't have come anyway
rows.explainer: Governments and other groups (Rare, WWF, TNC, the World Bank) reform fisheries too; some reforms would have come anyway. Our judgment, 60% (30% to 90%).

rows.label: Fisheries: EDF's share among the groups behind the reforms
rows.explainer: EDF's share among the outside groups and funders that design and negotiate the reforms. Fisheries ministries and fishers' cooperatives, who adopt and carry out the rules, are under the mobiliser's share, not here. EDF's teams lead the design and negotiation in the fisheries it counts; other groups and funders join. No published accounting of the outside support: our judgment, 50% (25% to 80%).

rows.label: Fisheries: share of credit used
Fisheries: share of the reforms enforced as written
rows.explainer: Small-scale fisheries rules are often weakly enforced. Our judgment, 50% (20% to 80%).

rows.label: Side effect: fishers squeezed out as access rights concentrate, as a share of the fisheries branch
rows.explainer: Tradable catch shares can concentrate quota in fewer boats, and some crew and small owners lose work; community-based rights, which EDF mostly backs in small-scale fisheries, do less of this. Our judgment, −5% of the branch (−15% to 0).

rows.label: Farm emissions: share of the cut that wouldn't have come anyway
rows.explainer: Fertiliser prices and companies' own supply-chain targets drive part of the change. Our judgment, 50% (20% to 80%).

rows.label: Farm emissions: EDF's share among the groups behind the cut
rows.explainer: EDF's share among the groups that research, advise and press for the practices and rules; farmers, agribusiness and governments, who carry them out, are under the mobiliser's share, not here. EDF is one of a handful of large environmental groups working with growers and food companies. No published accounting: our judgment, 35% (15% to 60%).

rows.label: Farm emissions: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among those who paid for or did the same work, times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out or adopt the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Farm emissions: share of the practices kept up
rows.explainer: USDA's climate-smart commodities programme was cancelled in 2025, and farmers drop practices when payments end. Our judgment, 40% (15% to 70%).

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): no death, IQ point, income or tonne is measured for EDF's work; the health figures are EPA's estimates of whole rules, the fisheries and farm reach our judgments. Every branch takes it.

rows.label: Other work of the period not modelled, as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: Left out of the branches: the Toxic Substances Control Act rules of 2024 (methylene chloride, trichloroethylene and perchloroethylene bans; EDF's chemicals team was central; since partly delayed), PFAS drinking-water limits (PFOA and PFOS kept, deadlines pushed to 2031), food and consumer chemicals, the lead-pipe rule's ADHD and birthweight benefits, water (Colorado River, California groundwater), coastal resilience (Louisiana's Mid-Barataria sediment diversion, cancelled in 2025: worth nothing now). Their spending is in the cost, so leaving them out would count them as worth nothing. Our judgment, 30% of the modelled value (10% to 80%): the soot and lead-pipe rules are the largest.
